title: Blood Supply of the Central Nervous System and Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows blood into the brain through the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems, maps each arterial territory onto the structures it feeds, and uses that map to predict cortical, lacunar, and brainstem stroke syndromes. It then traces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from secretion to absorption, follows venous blood out through the dural sinuses, and explains how the brain holds its blood flow steady and what happens when intracranial pressure rises. Board questions give a deficit, a ventricle pattern, or a set of vital signs and ask you to name the vessel, the site of obstruction, or the mechanism. Localization depends on knowing what lies where and which artery reaches it.
prerequisites: Lobes, gyri, motor and sensory homunculi, and language areas (NE-3)
Brainstem cross-sectional anatomy: cranial nerve nuclei and long tracts (NE-3, NE-7, NE-8)
Meninges, meningeal spaces, cisterns, and the blood-brain barrier (NE-4)
Mean arterial pressure, Poiseuille relationship, and the baroreceptor reflex (CV units)
CO2 transport and the bicarbonate buffer system

connections.how: The spaces CSF fills and the hemorrhages that occupy them are described there; this chapter adds the flow path and what blocks it.
Atherosclerosis, embolism, and hypertensive arteriolosclerosis produce the territorial and lacunar infarcts whose deficits are predicted here.
Hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, and herniation are the pathologies that raise intracranial pressure and lower perfusion pressure.
PaCO2, set by alveolar ventilation, is the strongest local regulator of cerebral vessel diameter, so breathing pattern changes brain blood volume.
The Cushing reflex combines the CNS ischemic response with the arterial baroreceptor reflex.

terms.def: The arterial ring at the base of the brain that links the two internal carotid systems with each other and with the vertebrobasilar system through communicating arteries.
An artery whose territory has no effective collateral supply, so its occlusion infarcts the tissue it feeds.
The border region between two arterial territories, the area most vulnerable when overall perfusion pressure falls.
A small deep infarct (under about 15 mm) from occlusion of a single penetrating artery, usually from hypertensive small vessel disease.
Cranial nerve signs on the side of a brainstem lesion combined with long tract signs on the opposite side of the body.
Ventricular dilation from obstruction within the ventricular system or its outlets, so the ventricles no longer communicate with the subarachnoid space.
Dilation of all four ventricles from impaired CSF absorption or flow in the subarachnoid space, with open ventricular pathways.
A valveless, endothelium-lined channel between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura that collects cerebral venous blood and CSF.
A superficial cerebral vein that crosses the subdural space to enter a dural sinus.
The intrinsic ability of cerebral arterioles to keep blood flow nearly constant across a wide range of perfusion pressure.
The pressure that drives blood through the brain, calculated as mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
Systemic hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing produced when raised intracranial pressure makes the brainstem ischemic.

sections.title: The circle of Willis and the cerebral arterial territories

blocks.text: The brain receives about 15% of resting cardiac output through two paired inflows. The internal carotid arteries form the anterior circulation; the vertebral arteries, branches of the subclavian arteries that ascend through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae and enter the skull through the foramen magnum, form the posterior circulation. The two vertebral arteries unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery, which runs up the ventral pons and divides at the midbrain into the two posterior cerebral arteries (PCA).

Each internal carotid artery ends by dividing into the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and the larger middle cerebral artery (MCA). The circle of Willis closes the ring: the anterior communicating artery joins the two ACAs, and each posterior communicating artery joins an internal carotid artery to the PCA on its side. A complete, well-sized circle is present in only a minority of people, so collateral capacity varies widely.

blocks.title: Assembly of the circle of Willis
steps: Vertebral arteries ascend and enter through the foramen magnum
Vertebrals unite at the pontomedullary junction as the basilar
Basilar divides at the midbrain into the two PCAs
Posterior communicating arteries join each PCA to the internal carotid
Each internal carotid divides into ACA and MCA
Anterior communicating artery joins the two ACAs
blocks.caption: The ring links right and left carotid systems with the vertebrobasilar system.

blocks.text: The circle protects against slow, proximal occlusion. When one internal carotid artery narrows gradually in the neck, flow can arrive from the opposite side through the anterior communicating artery or from the basilar through a posterior communicating artery. It cannot protect against sudden occlusion distal to the ring. Branches beyond the circle overlap only at their borders, and the penetrating arteries that enter deep gray matter are functional end arteries, so an embolus there produces a predictable infarct.

blocks.title: Cerebral arterial territories
rows: Medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes back to the parieto-occipital sulcus, including the paracentral lobule (leg and foot cortex); most of the corpus callosum
Most of the lateral convexity of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, including face and arm cortex, Broca and Wernicke areas, and the insula
Putamen, part of the globus pallidus and caudate, and much of the internal capsule
Occipital lobe including primary visual cortex, inferior and medial temporal lobe, splenium of the corpus callosum, thalamus and midbrain through perforating branches
blocks.caption: Superficial branches supply cortex and underlying white matter; deep perforators supply the basal ganglia, internal capsule, and thalamus.

blocks.text: The lenticulostriate arteries leave the MCA stem at nearly right angles and are small, so they receive nearly the full pressure of a large parent artery. Chronic hypertension thickens their walls with hyaline arteriolosclerosis and lipohyalinosis, which leads either to occlusion (lacunar infarct) or to rupture (hypertensive hemorrhage, most often in the putamen). The watershed zones between ACA and MCA and between MCA and PCA lie at the farthest reach of each tree, so they infarct first when systemic pressure falls, as in cardiac arrest or severe hypotension.

sections.title: Predicting cerebral and lacunar stroke syndromes

blocks.text: A stroke deficit is the function of the tissue that loses its blood supply. The motor and sensory homunculi are draped across two territories: the leg and foot area lies on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the ACA, while the trunk, arm, hand, and face areas lie on the lateral convexity, supplied by the MCA. The descending motor pathway crosses in the lower medulla and the ascending sensory pathways cross below the cortex, so a hemispheric infarct produces contralateral signs.

ACA occlusion therefore causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss of the leg more than the arm, with the face largely spared. Damage to the medial frontal lobe can add urinary incontinence and abulia (reduced drive and spontaneity). MCA occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss with less leg involvement. The face weakness is an upper motor neuron pattern that spares the forehead, because the facial nucleus neurons for the forehead receive corticobulbar input from both hemispheres. Damage to the frontal eye field turns the eyes toward the side of the lesion, and involvement of the optic radiation can add a contralateral visual field defect.

Which hemisphere is involved decides the cortical signs. Language is lateralized to the left hemisphere in nearly all right-handed people and most left-handed people. A dominant MCA infarct causes aphasia: superior division infarcts damage Broca area in the inferior frontal gyrus (nonfluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension), inferior division infarcts damage Wernicke area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus (fluent speech with poor comprehension), and stem occlusion causes global aphasia. A nondominant MCA infarct causes contralateral hemineglect, often with denial of the deficit.

PCA occlusion infarcts the primary visual cortex and causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Central vision is often spared because the occipital pole, where the macula is represented, frequently receives collateral flow from the MCA. A dominant PCA infarct that also involves the splenium can cause alexia without agraphia, and thalamic involvement adds contralateral sensory loss.

blocks.title: Cerebral stroke syndromes
rows: Contralateral leg and foot more than arm; face spared
Urinary incontinence, abulia, frontal release signs
Contralateral face and arm more than leg; lower face only
Aphasia if dominant; hemineglect if nondominant; gaze toward lesion; field defect
Usually none; thalamic sensory loss if perforators involved
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Lenticulostriate (lacune in posterior limb of internal capsule)
Pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm, and leg equally
No aphasia, neglect, or field defect
blocks.caption: Leg-predominant weakness points medially (ACA); face and arm predominance with cortical signs points laterally (MCA).

blocks.text: A lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule shows the opposite pattern from a cortical stroke. Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers for face, arm, and leg are packed into a few millimeters, so one small infarct weakens all three equally, while cortex is untouched and there is no aphasia, neglect, or field loss. The same small vessel disease in thalamic perforators causes pure sensory stroke.

blocks.title: Cortex or capsule?
blocks.text: A right-handed man has sudden weakness of the right face and arm, with the right leg only mildly weak, and he speaks in short, halting phrases but follows commands. Step 1: face and arm more than leg places the lesion on the lateral convexity, the MCA territory, not the ACA. Step 2: the deficit is on the right, so the lesion is in the left hemisphere. Step 3: impaired speech output with preserved comprehension is Broca aphasia, the inferior frontal gyrus, supplied by the superior division of the left MCA. If his face, arm, and leg were equally weak with normal language, the lesion would instead be a lacune in the left internal capsule.

The vertebrobasilar system feeds the brainstem through two kinds of branches. Paramedian branches (the anterior spinal artery in the medulla and pontine branches of the basilar) supply medial structures, and circumferential branches (posterior inferior cerebellar artery, PICA, from the vertebral; anterior inferior cerebellar artery, AICA, from the lower basilar; superior cerebellar artery from the upper basilar) supply the lateral brainstem and cerebellum.

Localization uses two rules. First, structures are arranged medially and laterally: the corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus are medial, while the spinothalamic tract, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, vestibular nuclei, nucleus ambiguus, cerebellar peduncles, and descending hypothalamic sympathetic fibers are lateral. Second, cranial nerve nuclei act on the same side, while the long tracts serve the opposite side of the body because they have already crossed (spinothalamic tract, medial lemniscus) or will cross below (corticospinal tract). One lesion therefore produces crossed findings, and the cranial nerve sign gives the level and side.

blocks.title: Brainstem stroke syndromes
rows: Loss of face pain and temperature (spinal trigeminal); Horner syndrome; dysphagia, hoarseness, reduced gag (nucleus ambiguus); limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle); vertigo, nystagmus, vomiting (vestibular nuclei)
Loss of body pain and temperature (spinothalamic)
Dysphagia and hoarseness; no limb weakness
Tongue weakness, deviates toward the lesion (CN XII)
Hemiparesis of arm and leg (pyramid); loss of vibration and position sense (medial lemniscus)

Whole-face lower motor neuron paralysis (facial nucleus); hearing loss and tinnitus (cochlear nuclei, labyrinthine artery); vertigo; face pain and temperature loss; Horner syndrome; ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle)
Loss of body pain and temperature
Bilateral: loss of facial, tongue, and swallowing movement; horizontal gaze often lost
Consciousness, blinking, and vertical eye movement preserved
blocks.caption: Medial syndromes take motor tracts and a motor cranial nerve; lateral syndromes take pain pathways, vestibular nuclei, cerebellar connections, and sympathetic fibers.

blocks.text: The lateral medullary syndrome is the classic crossed sensory pattern. Fibers for pain and temperature of the face descend in the spinal trigeminal tract on the same side before crossing, while body pain and temperature fibers crossed in the spinal cord and ascend in the lateral spinothalamic tract, so both lie in the lateral medulla and are lost on opposite sides. Weakness is absent because the pyramids are medial. Vertebral artery occlusion produces this syndrome at least as often as occlusion of PICA itself.

The medial medullary syndrome is a crossed motor pattern. The hypoglossal nerve exits medially between the pyramid and olive, so its fibers and the pyramid are damaged together: the tongue deviates toward the lesion while the opposite arm and leg are weak. The AICA syndrome resembles the PICA syndrome one level higher, with the facial nucleus and cochlear structures replacing the nucleus ambiguus. The facial weakness involves the forehead because the nucleus itself, the lower motor neuron, is destroyed.

In the locked-in syndrome, basilar occlusion infarcts the ventral pons bilaterally, interrupting corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers to all limbs and to the lower cranial nerves. The reticular activating system lies dorsally in the pontine and midbrain tegmentum and is spared, so the patient is fully awake. Vertical gaze and eyelid control depend on midbrain structures above the lesion, so blinking and vertical eye movement become the only means of communication.

sections.title: CSF production, circulation, and the site of obstruction

blocks.text: The choroid plexus, a fold of pia and capillaries covered by specialized ependymal epithelium, lies in the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles and produces most of the CSF, about 500 mL per day, so the roughly 150 mL in the system turns over several times daily. The epithelium secretes actively: Na+/K+-ATPase on the ventricular surface pumps Na+ into the ventricle, carbonic anhydrase supplies HCO3-, Cl- and HCO3- follow, and water moves through aquaporin-1 channels. Because secretion is active, production continues at nearly the same rate when outflow is blocked, so obstruction causes progressive dilation.

blocks.title: Path of CSF
steps: Choroid plexus secretes CSF into the lateral ventricles
Interventricular foramina (of Monro) to the third ventricle
Cerebral aqueduct through the midbrain
Fourth ventricle
Median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka)
Subarachnoid space and cisterns around brain and cord
Arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus
blocks.caption: CSF moves by bulk flow from secretion sites to venous absorption sites; the aqueduct is the narrowest channel.

blocks.text: Absorption occurs mainly through arachnoid granulations, tufts of arachnoid that project into the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus. They act as one-way valves: CSF passes into venous blood when CSF pressure exceeds sinus pressure, and blood cannot pass back. Absorption therefore rises with CSF pressure and falls when sinus pressure rises. Some CSF also leaves along cranial and spinal nerve sheaths to lymphatics.

Hydrocephalus is enlargement of the ventricles from excess CSF. The rule for localizing a block is that every ventricle upstream of the obstruction dilates, while every ventricle downstream stays normal or small. A block within the ventricles or at the fourth ventricle outlets is noncommunicating hydrocephalus. When the ventricular path is open but absorption at the granulations or flow through the subarachnoid space is impaired, all four ventricles enlarge, which is communicating hydrocephalus.

blocks.title: Site of obstruction and ventricular pattern
rows: Colloid cyst in the roof of the third ventricle
Congenital aqueductal stenosis; pineal region tumor
Lateral, third, and fourth (unless the tumor fills the fourth)
Scarring after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage
blocks.caption: Walk the path from the lateral ventricles downstream: dilation stops at the block.

blocks.text: The age of the patient shapes the presentation. Before the cranial sutures fuse, ventricular enlargement expands the skull, producing a rapidly enlarging head and a bulging fontanelle. After fusion the skull cannot expand, so pressure rises and causes headache, vomiting, and papilledema. Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a chronic communicating form in older adults with normal or intermittently raised pressure and the triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline, explained by stretch of periventricular corona radiata fibers. Ventricles also enlarge passively when brain tissue is lost, as in Alzheimer disease (hydrocephalus ex vacuo); pressure is normal and no flow is blocked.

blocks.predict: A pineal tumor compresses the cerebral aqueduct. Which ventricles enlarge, and why does CSF keep accumulating?
blocks.explain: The lateral and third ventricles enlarge because they are upstream; the fourth stays normal because it lies downstream. The choroid plexus keeps secreting actively regardless of back pressure, so volume and pressure continue to rise.

sections.title: Venous drainage, subdural hematoma, and dural sinus thrombosis

blocks.text: Cerebral veins and dural sinuses have no valves, so blood moves along pressure gradients toward the internal jugular veins. The sinuses lie between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura, and their rigid walls keep them open even when venous pressure is low. Emissary and diploic veins connect the sinuses with scalp veins, and the ophthalmic veins connect facial veins with the cavernous sinus, which gives infection a path inward.

blocks.title: Cerebral venous drainage
steps: Superficial cerebral veins cross the subdural space as bridging veins
Superior sagittal sinus along the falx cerebri
Deep internal cerebral veins form the great cerebral vein
Great cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus form the straight sinus
Superior sagittal and straight sinuses meet at the confluence
Transverse sinuses, then sigmoid sinuses
Internal jugular veins at the jugular foramina
blocks.caption: The cavernous sinus drains separately: superior petrosal sinus to the sigmoid sinus, inferior petrosal sinus to the internal jugular vein.

blocks.text: Bridging veins are the weak point. They run from the brain surface, which moves within the skull, to the sinus, which is fixed to the dura. Acceleration and deceleration of the head shear them. As the brain shrinks with age or chronic alcohol use, the veins are stretched across a wider subdural space and tear with milder force; in infants violent shaking produces the same injury. Blood collects between the dura and arachnoid at venous pressure, so it accumulates slowly over hours to weeks. Because the clot lies beneath the dura, the dural attachments at the sutures do not confine it, so it spreads along the convexity in a crescent and crosses suture lines, stopping only at dural reflections such as the falx and tentorium.

blocks.title: Subdural compared with epidural hematoma
rows: Middle meningeal artery, often with temporal bone fracture
blocks.caption: The bleeding vessel determines pressure and tempo; the dural attachments determine shape.

blocks.text: Dural venous sinus thrombosis follows the conditions of venous thrombosis in general: hypercoagulability (pregnancy and the postpartum period, estrogen-containing contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias, malignancy), slow flow (dehydration), and local injury or infection (mastoiditis spreading to the sigmoid or transverse sinus, facial infection spreading to the cavernous sinus). Occlusion raises pressure throughout the venous and capillary beds upstream.

blocks.title: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis raises intracranial pressure
steps: Thrombus occludes the superior sagittal sinus
Sinus pressure rises
CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations falls
Cortical venous pressure and capillary pressure rise
Vasogenic edema and venous infarcts, often hemorrhagic
Intracranial pressure rises: headache, papilledema, seizures
blocks.caption: Two mechanisms act together: CSF accumulates and venous congestion swells the brain.

blocks.text: Venous infarcts differ from arterial infarcts. They do not follow an arterial territory, they are often bilateral and parasagittal when the superior sagittal sinus is involved, and they frequently bleed because arterial inflow continues into tissue whose outflow is blocked.

sections.title: Regulation of cerebral blood flow, perfusion pressure, and the Cushing reflex

blocks.text: The brain is about 2% of body weight but receives roughly 50 mL of blood per 100 g of tissue per minute and stores almost no glucose or oxygen, so consciousness is lost within seconds when flow stops.

Autoregulation keeps flow nearly constant while mean arterial pressure (MAP) stays between about 60 and 150 mm Hg. Arteriolar smooth muscle constricts when stretched by higher pressure and dilates when pressure falls (the myogenic response), reinforced by local metabolites. Outside the range flow follows pressure passively, with ischemia below it and hyperperfusion and edema above it. Chronic hypertension shifts the curve to higher pressures, so a pressure that is normal for others can leave such a brain underperfused.

blocks.title: Local regulators of cerebral arteriolar diameter
rows: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and lowers perivascular pH
Constriction; flow and cerebral blood volume fall
Fall in PaO2 below about 50 mm Hg
Hypoxia; little effect above this level
K+, adenosine, nitric oxide, and H+ from active tissue
blocks.caption: PaCO2 is the dominant chemical regulator.

blocks.text: Carbon dioxide is the most powerful chemical regulator. It diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier, carbonic anhydrase converts it to H+ and HCO3- in the perivascular fluid, and the fall in pH relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle. H+ in arterial blood crosses the barrier poorly, so a metabolic acidosis affects cerebral vessels much less than an equal respiratory acidosis. A rise in PaCO2 from 40 to about 70 mm Hg roughly doubles cerebral blood flow. Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2, constricts the arterioles, and reduces cerebral blood volume and therefore intracranial pressure (ICP) within minutes, but excessive hypocapnia can lower flow enough to cause ischemia.

Because the skull is rigid, the volumes of brain, blood, and CSF must total a constant (the Monro-Kellie doctrine). An added mass is first offset by pushing CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space and venous blood out of the skull; once those reserves are used, small added volumes cause steep rises in pressure. Normal ICP in a supine adult is about 5 to 15 mm Hg. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) equals MAP minus ICP, so as ICP climbs toward MAP, perfusion fails even when blood pressure is normal.

blocks.title: Calculating perfusion pressure
blocks.text: A patient with a large hemorrhage has a blood pressure of 120/75 mm Hg and an ICP of 35 mm Hg. Step 1: MAP is about diastolic plus one third of pulse pressure, 75 + 45/3 = 90 mm Hg. Step 2: CPP = 90 minus 35 = 55 mm Hg, below the normal of about 70 to 90 mm Hg and near the lower limit of autoregulation, so the brain is at the edge of ischemia. Step 3: if ICP rose to 60 mm Hg with MAP unchanged, CPP would fall to 30 mm Hg, which is the situation the Cushing reflex tries to correct by raising MAP.

blocks.title: The Cushing reflex
steps: ICP rises toward MAP
CPP falls and the medulla becomes ischemic
Medullary vasomotor center drives sympathetic discharge
Systemic hypertension, often with wide pulse pressure
Baroreceptors sense hypertension; vagal output slows the heart
Higher MAP restores CPP until ICP rises further
blocks.caption: Hypertension is the ischemic response; bradycardia is the baroreceptor response to it.

blocks.text: The resulting Cushing triad is systemic hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration, the last from compression or ischemia of the pontine and medullary respiratory centers. It is a late sign of brainstem compromise and impending herniation.

blocks.predict: Why does hyperventilation lower ICP, while an equivalent metabolic alkalosis has little effect?
blocks.explain: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier, so hypocapnia raises perivascular pH, constricts arterioles, and reduces cerebral blood volume. Plasma HCO3- and H+ cross the barrier slowly, so arteriolar pH changes little.
blocks.check: The PaCO2 paragraph and the regulator table.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology combine in every localization question. The arterial map tells which structures share a blood supply, cross-sectional anatomy tells which tracts and nuclei sit together, and the crossing points of the pathways turn a set of deficits into a side and a level. Pathology supplies the mechanism: atherosclerosis and embolism at the large arteries and the heart give territorial infarcts, hypertensive arteriolosclerosis of perforators gives lacunes and putaminal hemorrhage, falling systemic pressure gives watershed infarcts, and the Virchow triad gives venous sinus thrombosis. Microbiology and immunology enter through meningitis, whose inflammatory exudate scars the arachnoid granulations, and through infections that spread inward along valveless veins.

The fluid compartments are linked because they share one rigid box. A blocked aqueduct, a clotted sinus, an expanding hematoma, or vasodilation from hypercapnia all add volume, raise ICP, and lower CPP, and the respiratory system influences that balance through PaCO2. Limits matter: arterial anatomy varies, so classic syndromes are often incomplete, and numerical ranges for autoregulation and ICP are approximate.

summary: Internal carotids give the ACA and MCA; vertebrals join as the basilar, which ends as the PCAs; communicating arteries complete the circle of Willis, which compensates only for slow proximal occlusion.
ACA feeds the medial frontal and parietal lobes (leg); MCA feeds the lateral convexity (face, arm, language); PCA feeds the occipital lobe and thalamus.
Lenticulostriate arteries are thin, high-pressure perforators damaged by hypertension, causing lacunes and putaminal hemorrhage.
Dominant MCA infarcts cause aphasia, nondominant MCA infarcts cause neglect, PCA infarcts cause homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, and a capsular lacune causes pure motor hemiparesis.

Brainstem lesions give ipsilateral cranial nerve signs and contralateral long tract signs; PICA means dysphagia and hoarseness, AICA means facial paralysis and deafness, medial medulla means tongue deviation, and basilar occlusion means locked-in.

CSF flows from the choroid plexus through the foramina of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct, fourth ventricle, and its apertures to the subarachnoid space and arachnoid granulations; ventricles upstream of a block dilate.
Bridging vein tears cause slowly accumulating crescentic subdural hematomas; sinus thrombosis raises ICP through impaired CSF absorption and venous congestion.
Autoregulation holds cerebral flow steady over a MAP of about 60 to 150 mm Hg; hypercapnia dilates and hypocapnia constricts cerebral arterioles.
CPP = MAP minus ICP; the Cushing reflex raises MAP to protect perfusion and produces hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing.

verify: The autoregulatory range is quoted as about 50 to 150, 60 to 140, or 60 to 150 mm Hg depending on the source; this chapter uses about 60 to 150 mm Hg.
The PaO2 at which cerebral vasodilation begins is quoted from about 50 to 60 mm Hg; confirm the value NABNE expects.
Normal CPP (about 70 to 90 mm Hg) and the CPP at which ischemia begins (about 50 to 60 mm Hg) are consensus approximations; confirm any cutoff NABNE tests.
The proportion of people with a complete circle of Willis varies widely between anatomical series; the chapter states only that it is a minority.
The doubling of cerebral blood flow when PaCO2 rises from 40 to about 70 mm Hg follows Guyton and Hall; other texts express the relationship as a percentage change per mm Hg.
Lacunar infarct size is usually defined as under 15 mm, though some sources use 20 mm.

Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Wallenberg (lateral medullary) and Dejerine (medial medullary) syndromes, Monro-Kellie doctrine, foramina of Monro, Magendie, and Luschka, and great vein of Galen, or only descriptive terms.
